reviews.text: Very fun game, works at launch, extremely stylish, resource management where the people and yourself are resources in a way that's reminiscent of Darkest Dungeon. Been looking for a scifi game where you aren't a space cop/soldier and this is refreshing. Social elements are light so far but still interesting, makes relationships more about trying to get more minions and reputation than actually getting to know the characters and their stories. Which could be unsatisfying but feels very in line with the setting and the well-crafted gameplay loop

I really like the concept of this game, and I'm excited to see how the story goes. There is replayability at least two times due to the different faction quests, but I think it would be really neat if there was a game mode unlocked after completing both storylines. This game is definitely not a roguelike but I think it could really benefit from a roguelike mode, with procedural quests and possibly even characters. One negative I have to say would be the combat, it's just not really fun or strategic. As far as I can tell there's no compendium of enemy types and moves, and you can't see the enemy's intents either, which makes things very hard. You pretty much have to just hit things until they die, which can take a while if there's a lot of enemies. Not being able to move past enemies makes the already small grid map feel very cramped as well. All in all, it's very interesting as an rpg in a space prison, but as a strategic fighting game, it's very lacking. I do find it to be worth putting up with the lackluster combat, though I will ALWAYS take a combat-free route if it presents itself.

The demo that I played of this game quite a while ago seemed like a good start. Unfortunately the full version seems like they didn't get very far past the demo, and it lacks the substance and balance it needs to be a good game. I played for about an hour and the promise that the game seemed to have in the demo just wasn't there anymore, and it wasn't really any fun to play. A big issue is that the game mechanics are pretty rudimentary and are not balanced well. One of the best examples of this is how poorly balanced the three character races are and how useless some of the class abilities are compared to others. It's like they had no time for testing, and did no balancing at all. The area for each turn based fight is just too small, it's often the same every time you get info a fight, and it is too frequently littered with "environmental hazards." The fights don't feel very tactical and the overall gameplay is repetitive - very repetitive. For some reason you can craft items but you cannot repair items you have crafted at the bench where you craft those items. Instead you have to pay someone to fix the items for you. This makes zero sense because if you know how to make something out of a pile of scrap you should be able to make repairs using more scrap. The writing isn't terrible but isn't very good either, not really engaging. The daily time limit, which limits the number of "nodes" you can travel, simply isn't long enough. It takes way too long to go to places that you should be able to easily visit 3 or 4 times in a day. For example you will waste almost an entire day going to the cafeteria ONCE and doing a few short encounters along the way. Based on the demo I expected a lot more from the full release and it did not deliver. I am refunding the game. It's about a 3/10 for me.

This isn't a bad game really, but it just doesn't quite hook me. The overall design is fine for a casual game but there are two main issues that prevent me from enjoying it. The first, and lesser issue, is that combat is a bit too simple for my taste. There isn't much to it strategically. It's fine for a casual game, and if this was my only issue, I'd probably keep playing to at least finish one playthrough and give it a thumbs up. The bigger problem for me is the inventory system. A lot of the game is about gathering crafting components and using them at various crafting spots to turn them into other things, but you have limited inventory and going between locations is expensive in in-game time. They give you little cubbies all over the map to stash a few items, and a slightly larger one in your prison cell (home base), but honestly it's just really tedious being inventory restricted in a game that wants you to collect 1-2 at a time of a few different things on each map and somehow also have room for the things you're crafting. It's just frustrating trying to rearrange inventory space between home base and cubbies and your personal inventory. Unlimited personal inventory would have fixed the issue and probably made the difference in my review. But I just don't want to engage with that mechanic any more.

Space Prison is an RPG with turn-based combat, in which you are a prisoner trying to escape from… well, a space prison. It’s an incredibly fun concept that’s rarely ever done, if at all, however, it does not feel like the game is taking full advantage of its premise. The prison doesn’t feel much like a prison and you’re not really doing anything to escape it. What you do is join one of two prison gangs and move up the ladder by completing jobs for fellow gang members to earn their respect, so you can challenge gang members of higher rank to take their place. There are several locations in the game with rogue-like corridors between them filled with random fights/loot/events. The combat is turn-based and you’ll usually have some pet rats, drones or befriended gang members with you, but it’s all rather simple and limited tactic-wise. There’s a strong emphasis on crafting, and your biggest enemy through the entire game is your limited inventory space. Overall, Space Prison is a rather simple game with cute art. Not especially great, but kinda fun and, in a way, charming.

Space Prison, developed by Wooden Alien and published by Firesquid, is a refreshingly original take on the tactical RPG and survival genre, set within the grimy, claustrophobic corridors of a futuristic intergalactic penitentiary. The game blends social simulation, turn-based combat, and resource management into a cohesive and engaging package, driven by its imaginative setting and sharp, often darkly humorous tone. From the moment you begin your sentence in this alien lock-up, you're introduced to a world where survival is far more than a matter of brute strength—it’s about alliances, subversion, smart planning, and the constant weighing of risk and reward. As an inmate in this sprawling space prison, you begin by selecting from one of several alien species, each with their own biological strengths, weaknesses, and social modifiers. This choice is meaningful, shaping not just your combat capabilities but also how other inmates perceive and interact with you. You’re also assigned a criminal background, which adds additional perks and narrative flavor, further personalizing your character and playstyle. Once inside, you’re quickly introduced to the layered systems that define the game: gang politics, crafting, combat, questing, and the delicate maintenance of relationships with other inmates and factions. This isn't a game where violence alone will carry you through. Influence, respect, and social maneuvering are just as important as a strong right hook. The prison itself is a fascinating setting—not just in terms of its visual design, which mixes brutalist sci-fi architecture with quirky alien elements, but also in the way it functions as a living ecosystem. Inmates follow routines, gangs enforce territories, and opportunities constantly emerge for both gain and danger. As you explore and engage with this world, you’ll need to balance your time between gathering contraband, completing favors for fellow prisoners, upgrading your cell with useful tools or hidden stashes, and preparing for turn-based skirmishes. The social dynamics play a significant role; aligning with a gang can offer protection and bonuses, but it also paints a target on your back from rival groups. Similarly, helping a fellow inmate might open new opportunities—or earn the ire of someone with more power than you can handle. Combat is where the game shows its tactical depth. It’s turn-based, grid-driven, and surprisingly strategic given the confined nature of its environments. Weapons are often improvised—shanks, modified tools, or black-market tech—and positioning matters greatly. Cover, line-of-sight, and environmental hazards all play a role in how fights unfold. The game encourages smart planning over reckless aggression, especially since injury or death can have lasting consequences. That said, dying doesn't end the game outright. One of the more creative mechanics is the mind transfer system, allowing your consciousness to be uploaded into a new body upon death. While you retain much of your progress, some relationships and abilities might be lost or changed, which gives each run a slightly roguelike flavor and makes death something to be feared but not game-ending. Outside of combat, the survival elements keep the pressure on. Food, resources, and crafting materials must be acquired either through exploration, trade, or less-than-legal means. Upgrading your cell isn’t just cosmetic—it becomes your operational hub, where you can craft better gear, hatch escape plans, or simply rest and recover. There’s also an element of pet management with space rats, strange little creatures that can assist in various ways depending on how you raise and treat them. These small touches add a bit of levity and warmth to an otherwise tense environment, and they help flesh out the game's tone, which balances gritty sci-fi tension with moments of irreverent humor. Visually, the game adopts a clean, stylized aesthetic that evokes graphic novels and animated series, favoring bold outlines and saturated colors. It manages to convey the oppressive atmosphere of incarceration without becoming visually monotonous. The sound design, meanwhile, reinforces the game’s mood, with a subtle ambient soundtrack that shifts depending on time of day, gang activity, and danger levels. Voice acting is minimal but effective where used, allowing players to fill in the emotional gaps through strong writing and reactive NPC behavior. However, the game isn’t without its flaws. Being a relatively new release, some interface elements could use refinement, particularly in inventory management and map navigation. There are also moments when pacing becomes uneven—especially during longer stretches between major narrative or combat events. The core loop of scavenging, upgrading, and managing alliances remains engaging for quite a while, but players who prefer a constant stream of action may find it drags in places. Additionally, while the mind transfer system alleviates the sting of death, some might find that it lowers the stakes a bit too much after a few cycles, turning what was once tense into routine. Despite these minor drawbacks, Space Prison stands out as one of the more creative indie strategy titles of the year. It succeeds in delivering a world that feels dangerous, lived-in, and full of narrative potential. Every decision, from whom you befriend to what you hide in your locker, can ripple outward and change how your story unfolds. Whether you’re trying to rise through the ranks of the prison's power structure, quietly gather intel for an escape plan, or simply survive your sentence with your mind and body intact, the game offers enough tools and freedom to support a variety of approaches. It’s a bold debut from Wooden Alien, and with continued support and updates, Space Prison has the potential to become a cult classic among fans of tactical RPGs and immersive survival sims alike. Rating: 8/10

Has some nifty ideas and concepts, though the game is very basic at the end of the day. Once you've done a few days in game you've basically seen all the game has to offer as far as gameplay goes; you get 8 hours every day to do what you want, which are usually spent traveling from one hub to the next. You'll be balancing keeping your health, hunger, and hope up while leveling up your equipment, stations, and rising in the ranks of your chosen gang. I'll get the negative out of the way first. Inventory management has some really neat ideas, namely the contraband system where items with a yellow background are confiscated if you're caught with them in your inventory. You can hide a few items in secret pockets, but the rest will be seen by guards and sensors. This is fine, the only trouble is the storage you do get in the game is woefully inadequate. Your main storage in your cell doesn't offer you much room to keep items, even in the mid game you will find yourself running out of space to keep your stuff and a lot of resource based quests are time sensitive, so you end up hording everything without many uses for them. You can make secret stashes in certain facilities, but even these can only hold 4 items at a time and you still have to deal with sensors and guards for the contraband issue. I feel it would've been better if items were more precious in the game, my inventory and storage is overflowing with stuff and I have no real way of getting rid of the useless stuff anymore. The rest of the game is pretty easy and straight forward. The only enemies that really give me any trouble are the guards who have powerful attacks that bypass your armor and have a good chance to stun you, and even if they don't stun they block a random skill from being used for at least 1 turn. Other than that every fight has been really one sided and easy, I rarely even have to heal my character. The part of the game I enjoy the most by far is earning the loyalty of fellow gang members and rising up the ranks. Each gang member requires you to complete their quest chain, some need you to complete an investigation into the corruption of the prison, others need your help getting them a job in the prison, etc. None of them are particularly deep, but it's the fun of seeing them grow comfortable with you and getting them as permanent party members as you go that's so rewarding. Beating a higher ranked gang member in a fight earns you their spot and they're knocked down to your previous rank. The idea is to become the boss of your gang and take over the prison. The most unique part of the game imo is how "respawning" works. Every prisoner is equipped with a collar that captures their consciousness when they die, and are placed onto a new body when the old one dies. So narratively, you can't just get killed to escape your sentence, you'll just be placed in a new body. My character died after having to fight three guards in a row, and I was placed in a new alien body and I had to get all my old stuff from the morgue. It's neat, though not thoroughly explored in game. Overall this is a solid 7/10 for me. It's surprisingly chill for the setting it has and you have a lot of control over your life in the game, but I'm enjoying what's here. I'd get it on sale or at least try the demo to see if you like it. You don't get to explore the gang life in the demo, but you get the gist of the gameplay.

[h2]A Decent But Somewhat Underwhelming Jailbreak[/h2] Space Prison blends survival game elements with turn-based RPG combat. This game is a fun and relatively short blend of these two genres, and certain questlines and easter eggs (such as the Steamy Games posters) show that the developers channeled some real passion into the project. Pretty much everything about this game was handled competently, but few of its parts are particularly gripping. There are also a lot of things that feel underdeveloped. The biggest choice you make in the early game is which of the two prison gangs to join as you build up your reputation. There is, however, little practical difference between them: their hideouts offer almost identical resources and crafting options. There was one notable exception: Gravity Fist allows you to make a fortified stun baton that trivializes virtually all the late game combat, and Hypernova doesn't have that crafting option. But otherwise, there's little practical difference between them. This made my second playthrough somewhat disappointing. Combat is interesting at first but gets repetitive. The combat arenas are all very small, so tactical options are somewhat limited. But since your stats are (except for the early game) far superior to most enemies, you're generally be fine just duking it out against the competition. Exploration is reasonably well-paced, although you will end up visiting the same places many times. I found the survival elements (that is, the Hope and Hunger meters) very easy to manage: they were almost always near the max. On that note, I will share one oddity. In my first playthrough (on Normal), I never died. Once that playthrough was done, I rolled immediately into Broken Collar mode (which appears identical to Normal except that you have one life), and I completed that run easily as well. I'm not saying this to brag: the game simply isn't that hard. It implements a reverse difficulty curve where almost all the challenge is in the first 6-10 fights where you have few allies and resources. By the end of the game, you're deploying gang members, rats, drones, and various combinations thereof to help out, and the enemies just don't hit hard enough to put up much resistance. As long as you craft suitable equipment and use the resources you find, you'll be fine. I will also note that there appear to be two bugged achievements. There is one for maxing out your cooking workbench and a similar one for the engineer's workbench, but I never found any workbenches by those names. I suspect they existed in an earlier version of the game and have since been removed. So how would I appraise the game overall? I think it could be a decent entry point for folks unfamiliar with these kind of turn-based RPGs, and there are some amusing questlines and such that make for a decent distraction. That said, it's hard to imagine most enjoying more than one playthrough in this game, which would last 12-15 hours. It's good enough to recommend, but I would only buy this on sale: it is not worth $20. Overall: 6.5 / 10
